Background
Introductory Concepts and Terminology

COVID-19 Pandemic
• The COVID-19 Pandemic led to, arguably, the largest educational disruption in
the history of the United States.
• Nearly 3 years into the pandemic and the impacts of the pandemic are still being
felt.
• The pandemic impacted students academically, emotionally, physically, and
financially.
• In this overview, we address three things:
• Academic Impact: What is it and what happened to students in New
Hampshire?
• Academic Recovery: What is it and what is happening to students in New
Hampshire currently?
• Now What?: How can impact and recovery data be leveraged to help
students going forward? Evidence-based investigations of what is working.

What is Academic Impact?
What is Academic Recovery?
• The pandemic and all the ensuing disruptions functioned/functions
as an academic headwind, impeding (in general) the academic
progress of students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
▪ They slow one’s rate of progress (speedometer)
▪ And by slowing one’s rate of progress they lead to less distance being travelled
(odometer).
• In education odometer is to attainment as speedometer is to growth.
• Academic impact is analogous to a headwind, decreasing the rate of
student learning (deceleration) which, in turn leads to lower
attainment

What is Academic Impact?
What is Academic Recovery?
• Academic recovery is analogous to an academic tailwind,
increasing the rate of student learning (acceleration) which, in
turn leads to higher attainment.
• During Fall 2021 to present, under the presumption that student
education got back to normal, the hope was that rates of learning
stabilized to pre-pandemic rates or, even better, increased to rates
exceeding pre-pandemic rates allowing students to catch-up.
• Examination of academic impact/recovery are opposite sides of
the same coin and utilize the same analytics.

Impact & Recovery
• We investigate impact/recovery in two ways:
• Change in same grade/same cohort attainment: We examine equi-percentile
change in attainment. Impact: 2019 to 2021, Recovery 2021 to 2022
• Change in student growth: We examine change in baseline (pre-pandemic)
student growth (SGPs). Impact: 2019 to 2021 (using 2017 to 2019 growth
norms), Recovery: 2021 to 2022 (using 2018 to 2019 growth norms).

Assessment Data
• We investigated the impacts in achievement and growth of the pandemic across
two time frames:
• Impact: Spring 2020 through Summer 2021
• Recovery: Fall 2021 through Summer 2022
• To investigate impact we utilized two primary sources of data
• State summative assessment data (NH-SAS)
• Impact: NH-SAS Spring 2019 to Spring 2021 (NH-SAS testing cancelled in
• Recovery: NH-SAS Spring 2021 to Spring 2022
• State English Language Proficiency Data (ACCESS)
• Impact: ACCESS Winter 2020 to Winter 2021
• Recovery: ACCESS Winter 2021 to Winter 2022

Recovery Phase
• During the 2021-2022 academic year, school returned to normal for most students.
• The 2022-2023 academic year saw continued that trend.
• The hope was that a return to normal would lead recovery of the academic losses
incurred by students.
• Because learning slowed during the initial phase of the pandemic, to make up for
those losses, learning must accelerate to rates above normal in order to catch-up
for those loses.
• Data from two sources was utilized to examine whether recovery is occurring:
• NH-SAS data from 2021, 2022 and 2023
• WIDA-ACCESS data from 2021, 2022 and 2023

Recovery Phase: Cautions in Interpretation
• Interpretation of “recovery” based upon outcomes from tests can be misleading.
• Since NCLB, interpretation of education system quality is often based upon attainment of students
(e.g., Percentage of proficient students)
• Because student attainment dropped precipitously in New Hampshire (and nationwide) and has
not yet recovered to pre-pandemic percentages, there is a common misunderstanding that the
education system continues to suffer from the pandemic.
• To provide the appropriate nuance to understand academic recovery we distinguish between:
• Student Recovery: Are students back to levels of attainment they would have been had the
pandemic not occurred?
• Education System Recovery: Is the system back to supporting rates of learning observed
before the pandemic?
• NOTE: student learning (i.e., student growth) precedes student attainment. Higher/lower rates of
learning lead to high/low attainment.

2021-2022 & 2022-23: Recovery Phase
• Overall results suggest that New Hampshire students are experiencing something resembling a U-
shaped recovery.
• Depending upon how gradual the U-shaped recovery, the time-span needed to fully recovery may
extend beyond the amount of time
• The education system has recovered and is actually performing slightly better than it had
historically. in that it has returned to rates of learning that it produced pre-pandemic.
• It is critical to note that system level recovery is not the same as student recovery.
• Because student learning was significantly depressed between 2019 and 2021. Student recovery
will require rates of learning well in excess of what was typical pre-pandemic.
• Compared to results the Center has modeled in a dozen other states, New Hampshire is at or near
the top in terms of how it’s system and students are faring.
• Averages can obscure important variability. Whereas some students are faring well, others
struggle.

2021-2022 & 2022-23: Recovery Phase
• Results from 2023 following those in 2022 suggest New Hampshire is on the right path.
• In both ELA and mathematics, rates of learning returned to historical (pre-pandemic
norms) and in many grades exceeded pre-pandemic rates of learning. This increase in
rates of learning beyond pre-pandemic is helping students recover and to gradually
catch-back-up.
• The education system has recovered and is actually performing slightly better than it had
historically. in that it has returned to rates of learning that it produced pre-pandemic.
• It is critical to note that system level recovery is not the same as student recovery.
• Because student learning was significantly depressed between 2019 and 2021. Student
recovery will require rates of learning well in excess of what was typical pre-pandemic.
• Students not making sufficient progress eventually run out of time needed to catch-up.
